normalized.governing_thought: Enter the US in 2027 through Amazon, not national retail, and hold ad costs near the pilot's 28% so it pays back by 2030
executive_summary: The US is worth entering: K-beauty skincare nearly doubled to $3.6B, and Onsoo's Amazon test sells (61% of K-beauty buyers buy mostly on Amazon; Pilot sales nearly doubled in six months)
Amazon-led entry fits the cash cap easily but pays back by 2030 only if ad costs stay near the pilot's (Payback needs ACoS of 28.6% or less; About $26M of revenue in 2030, not $40M)
Retail-led entry fails the board's tests even on the planning team's own inputs (Newcomers like Onsoo sell 2.6 units a door a week; Cash outflow passes the $18M cap in 2029)
A Japan scale-up is safer but adds only $7M of revenue in 2030, in a slow market (Japan pays back in 2029, with $1.8M by 2030)
Launch on Amazon in 2027 under an ad-cost ceiling; add retail only once awareness passes 20% (Ambition restated: about $26M by 2030)

slides.title: Entering the US market
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Onsoo enter the US market in 2027, and if so by which route, within an $18M cash cap, payback by 2030 and an 8% group margin floor?
evidence: Success criteria: Cumulative US cash outflow of no more than $18M through 2030; Cumulative US cash back to zero by the end of 2030; Group operating margin at or above 8% in every year; A US business on the way to $40M of revenue by 2030; Only one major new-market launch in 2027
Decision maker: CEO and board of Onsoo Botanicals
Timing: Board meeting, March 2027
Out of scope: Mass-retail or DTC-led entry; US acquisition or distributor; US and Japan launches together in 2027

slides.title: The US opportunity
The US is worth entering: K-beauty skincare is growing fast, its buyers shop online, and Onsoo already sells there

evidence: 61% of US K-beauty buyers buy K-beauty on Amazon most often

claims.claim: The Amazon pilot grew every month at a 4.5-star rating, although repeat purchase is well below Korea's
evidence: 1.9x June 2026 pilot units as a multiple of January's

Amazon-led entry fits easily within the cash cap, but pays back by 2030 only if ad costs stay near the pilot's

evidence: $4.7 contribution per cream at the plan's 25% ACoS

claims.claim: Peak cash need stays far below the $18M cap, but payback by 2030 needs ACoS to average 28.6% or less
evidence: 32% median ACoS of skincare brands scaling from $5M to $20M a year on Amazon

claims.claim: Revenue reaches about $26M in 2030 on plan, two-thirds of the board's ambition

slides.title: 2a: At the planning team's ad cost, Onsoo keeps about $4.73 of each $24 cream after Amazon's fees and advertising

claims.claim: Amazon takes most of the price, and ads are the biggest piece

Fulfillment: a fixed fee per unit, so larger pack sizes or bundles would dilute it
Product, freight and duty: less than a fifth of the price, so the tariff matters less than ad cost
evidence: referral fee 15% of price, duty 15% of ex-factory cost, advertising = ACoS × price

slides.title: 2b: To pay back by 2030, Amazon ad spend must average 28.6% of sales or less, about what the pilot achieved

alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: payback holds while ACoS averages 28.6% or less; the only option that meets the cash, payback and margin tests while building a US business

alternatives_considered.option: Option B: retail-led (national specialty retail) entry
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject: fails cash, payback and margin even on plan inputs; breaches the $18M cash cap in 2029, group margin below 8% in 2027–29; 4.5 units/door assumption and 1.3x halo challenged
Defer: safe, but leaves the US ambition untouched; adds only $7M of 2030 revenue in a market growing 1.5% a year; decide in 2028

alternatives_considered.option: Retail trigger at 15% aided awareness and national specialty retail from 2029 (CEO's proposal)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Replaced by 20% awareness, test doors first then roll out, and a sell-through check of at least 4.0 units per door a week
Left out: not modeled by the planning team; the two channels carry 26% of K-beauty skincare sales against Amazon's 41% (out of scope)
Left out: no inputs in the briefing pack; outside the options the board asked us to compare (out of scope)

alternatives_considered.option: US and Japan launches together in 2027

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The 28.6% threshold holds only if the plan's volumes do: 300,000 units in 2027 rising to 1.1 million in 2030, with four more SKUs
Every SKU earns the hero cream's per-unit economics, as the planning team assumes
Duty stays at 15%; at 25% the threshold falls by about 1.5 percentage points
The pilot ran at 28% on a small budget; the scaling benchmark is 32%
Ad cost at scale: ACoS rises to the 32% benchmark instead of falling to 25% (−$4.7M)
Tariff rise: duty on Korean cosmetics rises from 15% to 25% in mid-2027 (−$1.1M); both risks together leave Option A at −$3.4M
Repeat purchase stays at 29% as SKUs are added (not quantified); unclear whether more SKUs lift it
Korean-only labels keep drawing complaints (not quantified)
Exchange rate: upside only; left out of the case
Four brands are a pattern, not proof
Treat the halo as a hypothesis to test in a few doors, not as a planning input

Model simplifications: inventory of four months of landed cost is the only working capital; one-time costs expensed when incurred; Option J cash equals operating result; tax, financing, exchange-rate moves and any value after 2030 left out
Aided awareness survey (US women aged 18–44) is narrower than Table 8's category buyers
Synthetic benchmark data: company, competitors and figures are fictional
